body:
Regional kingdoms between the 8th and 12th centuries

Several powerful dynasties developed across the subcontinent during the early-medieval period. Their territorial bases differed, but they shared important features: control of agricultural resources, military competition, relationships with subordinate chiefs and support for religious or cultural institutions.

Three especially important powers were the Gurjara-Pratiharas of western and northern India, the Palas of Bengal and Bihar, and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan. The Cholas became another major power in the Tamil region.

DynastyPrincipal regionImportant association
Gurjara-PratiharaWestern and northern India, including Rajasthan and adjoining areasNorthern Indian power; contest for Kanauj
PalaBengal and BiharDharmapala; support for Buddhist institutions
RashtrakutaDeccanDantidurga; rivalry with the northern powers
CholaTamil region and Kaveri deltaVijayalaya, Rajaraja I and Rajendra I

Why Kanauj was important

Kanauj, in the Ganga valley of present-day Uttar Pradesh, became a highly valued political centre. Its location was associated with the agriculturally productive northern plains and important routes connecting different regions.

Control over Kanauj could provide access to resources and strengthen a ruler's political prestige. It was therefore attractive not only to neighbouring states but also to ambitious dynasties whose principal territories lay far away.

The tripartite struggle

The tripartite struggle was the prolonged contest among the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas for political control over Kanauj.

The word tripartite means involving 3 parties. In this case, it identifies the competing dynasties, not 3 different cities.

The struggle unfolded over several generations rather than in one battle. The contending rulers formed alliances, led military expeditions and challenged one another's authority. Control shifted, and none of the 3 parties permanently eliminated the others during the struggle.

The contest also demonstrates that regional kingdoms were not isolated. A Deccan-based ruler could intervene in northern Indian politics, while eastern and western Indian dynasties competed for the same strategic centre.

Important rulers

Dharmapala was an important Pala ruler associated with attempts to extend Pala influence into northern India. Vatsaraja and Nagabhata II are associated with Gurjara-Pratihara expansion, while Dhruva and Govinda III were important Rashtrakuta rulers who intervened in northern affairs. For a basic prelims understanding, their dynasty and regional association matter more than a detailed sequence of campaigns.

The Cholas as a regional comparison

In the south, Vijayalaya Chola captured the Kaveri delta from the Muttaraiyar chiefs during the middle of the 9th century and established his authority at Thanjavur. The earlier Muttaraiyar chiefs had been subordinate to the Pallavas.

Rajaraja I, who became king in 985 CE, expanded the Chola kingdom and strengthened its administration. His son Rajendra I continued its expansion and led expeditions that included the Ganga valley and overseas regions. The Chola example shows how successful state formation could combine agricultural resources, organised administration and military expansion.

The Cholas were a major contemporary regional dynasty, but they were not one of the 3 parties in the tripartite struggle for Kanauj.

Political and cultural consequences

Regional competition encouraged rulers to build forts, maintain armies, appoint officials and seek support from influential groups. Rulers also patronised temples and monasteries. Such institutions could receive land and become important centres of education, craft production and economic activity.

The Palas are especially associated with Buddhist monastic and artistic traditions in eastern India. The Rashtrakutas are associated with the remarkable Kailasanatha temple at Ellora, a major rock-cut monument. These cultural associations are useful because questions may match a dynasty with a region or monument rather than ask only about warfare.

Prelims focus

  • The tripartite struggle concerned control over Kanauj.
  • Its 3 parties were the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas.
  • The Palas were principally associated with Bengal and Bihar; the Rashtrakutas with the Deccan.
  • Dharmapala belonged to the Pala dynasty; Dantidurga to the Rashtrakuta dynasty.
  • Vijayalaya Chola established his authority at Thanjavur in the middle of the 9th century.
  • Trap: The Cholas were not a party to the tripartite struggle, despite being a major regional power.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 2, 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed pp. 16–24; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, ch. 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture', printed pp. 85–86 and 91–92.]

pictures.caption: The 3 powers competing for Kanauj.

title: The Great Regional Dynasties and the Tripartite Struggle for Kanauj

body:
Who were the Rajputs?

The term Rajput is derived from the Sanskrit word rajaputra, meaning son of a ruler. Between approximately the 8th and 14th centuries, it came to be associated more broadly with warriors, chiefs, commanders and ruling families claiming Kshatriya status.

The Rajputs did not constitute one united kingdom. Different Rajput clans and ruling houses controlled territories in Rajasthan, Gujarat, central India and other parts of northern India. They sometimes formed alliances, but they also fought one another over land, forts and political influence.

Rajput political power developed through control of territory, military organisation, relationships with local chiefs and recognition of royal authority. Some dynasties began as subordinate chiefs and became independent when stronger overlords weakened.

Important clans, kingdoms and centres

Questions about Rajput polities often depend on correctly matching a ruling house with its principal region, centre or important ruler.

Ruling houseRegion or centreImportant association
Chahamanas or ChauhansShakambhari, Ajmer and Delhi regionPrithviraja III; battles of Tarain
ParamarasMalwa; DharRaja Bhoja
ChandelasJejakabhukti or Bundelkhand; Khajuraho and KalinjarKhajuraho temples
GuhilasMewar; Chittor regionEarly-medieval ruling tradition of Mewar
GahadavalasKanauj and VaranasiChandradeva and Jayachandra

The Gahadavalas are included here as an important contemporary northern Indian regional dynasty. The term Rajput should not be used to imply that every dynasty in the table shared the same origin or political organisation.

Chahamanas of Shakambhari and Ajmer

The Chahamanas, also called Chauhans, developed power in parts of present-day Rajasthan and the Delhi region. The Shakambhari branch was associated with the area around Sambhar. Ajayaraja is associated with the establishment of Ajayameru, later known as Ajmer.

The best-known Chahamana ruler was Prithviraja III. His rivalry with Muhammad Ghori led to the battles of Tarain in 1191 and 1192.

Paramaras of Malwa

The Paramaras ruled in the Malwa region of central India. Their important political and cultural centre was Dhar. The ruler Bhoja became particularly well known for his patronage of learning and cultural activity.

The essential ruler-place association is Bhoja and Dhar, not Bhoja and Kanauj.

Chandelas of Jejakabhukti

The Chandelas controlled Jejakabhukti, broadly corresponding to the Bundelkhand region. Kalinjar was an important fortified centre, while Khajuraho became famous for its temples and sculpture.

The Khajuraho temples illustrate the close relationship between royal patronage, religious institutions and monumental architecture. The region contains both Hindu and Jaina temple traditions.

Forts, armies and political rivalry

Forts were important because they could protect a ruler's court, treasury, population and surrounding territory. Control of a fortified centre helped a dynasty maintain authority over nearby routes and settlements.

Early-medieval armies included cavalry, infantry and, in many cases, elephants. Kings also relied on subordinate chiefs who supplied soldiers. This arrangement could bring together considerable military strength, but its effectiveness depended on the loyalty and cooperation of the participating chiefs.

Wars were fought for political authority, agricultural resources, trade routes, forts and prestige. Rivalries between neighbouring kingdoms could make it difficult to maintain a lasting united military front.

Culture and the image of kingship

Rulers supported temples, scholars, poets and other specialists. Courtly literature often praised courage, loyalty and generosity. Such praise helped establish a ruler's reputation, but it should not be confused with a neutral account of every event.

The connections between Chandelas and Khajuraho, Paramaras and Dhar, and Chahamanas and Ajmer are especially useful for recognising the cultural and political geography of the period.

Prelims focus

  • Rajput is derived from rajaputra, meaning son of a ruler.
  • Chahamanas are associated with Shakambhari, Ajmer and Prithviraja III.
  • Paramara ruler Bhoja is associated with Dhar in Malwa.
  • Chandelas are associated with Jejakabhukti, Khajuraho and Kalinjar.
  • Gahadavalas are associated with Kanauj and Varanasi.
  • Trap: Rajput polities were separate kingdoms and clans, not one centrally governed Rajput empire.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Tracing Changes Through a Thousand Years', printed pp. 7–8; ch. 2, 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed pp. 20–21; GCERT, Social Science, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Rajput Age: New Ruler and States', sections on northern Indian states; GCERT, History, Class 11, ch. 13, 'Rajput States of India', printed pp. 101–103; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, ch. 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture', printed pp. 73–74.]

pictures.caption: A fortified centre in an early-medieval Rajput polity.

title: Rajput Polities: Clans, Warfare, Forts and Cultural Centres

body:
Why Gujarat matters in this period

Gujarat occupied an important position in early-medieval India because of its agricultural settlements, trading connections and regional kingdoms. Its rulers supported religious institutions, towns, reservoirs and temples. Gujarat was also affected by military campaigns coming from north-western India.

Three ruling houses are particularly useful for understanding the broad political sequence: the Chavdas, the Chaulukyas or Solankis, and the Vaghelas.

The Chavdas and Anhilwad Patan

The Chavdas were an important early ruling family associated with northern Gujarat. Vanraj Chavda is traditionally credited with founding Anhilwad Patan, also called Anahilapataka or Anhilavada, around 756 CE.

The city later became a major political and cultural centre under the Chaulukyas. Its importance illustrates how a regional capital could remain prominent even when the ruling dynasty changed.

The Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty

The Chaulukyas, commonly called the Solankis of Gujarat, rose to power in the 10th century. Mularaja is generally recognised as the founder of their ruling line in Gujarat.

Important Chaulukya rulers included Bhima I, Siddharaja Jayasimha and Kumarapala. Their reigns are associated with territorial authority, patronage of learning and the growth of important religious and architectural centres.

Chaulukyas of Gujarat and the earlier Chalukyas of Badami in Karnataka must be distinguished by region and historical context. Similar names do not make every ruler or event interchangeable.

Bhima I and Modhera

The Sun Temple at Modhera, in present-day Mehsana district, is associated with the reign of Bhima I and dates to approximately 1026 CE. It is an important example of the temple-building tradition of western India.

The complex includes a stepped water tank called the Surya Kund, an assembly hall and the main shrine. The tank contains 108 miniature shrines arranged among its steps.

Modhera is useful for connecting a ruler, a dynasty, a place and an architectural monument: Bhima I, Chaulukya or Solanki, Modhera and the Sun Temple.

Rani ki Vav at Patan

Rani ki Vav is a monumental stepwell at Patan dating to the 11th century. It is traditionally associated with Queen Udayamati and the memory of her husband, Bhima I.

A stepwell combines access to water with an elaborate architectural setting. Rani ki Vav is particularly known for its sculptural decoration and stepped construction. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014.

Siddharaja Jayasimha and Kumarapala

Siddharaja Jayasimha strengthened Chaulukya political authority and is remembered for patronage of learning. The Jain scholar Hemachandra was an important intellectual figure associated with the Chaulukya court and its cultural environment.

Kumarapala was another important Chaulukya ruler associated with Hemachandra and the patronage of Jain traditions. These links show how rulers supported influential scholars and religious institutions in addition to exercising military and administrative power.

The Vaghelas and the later transition

As Chaulukya power weakened, the Vaghelas, who had previously served as powerful chiefs connected with the Chaulukya political order, rose to prominence in Gujarat.

The sequence is important because it illustrates a broader early-medieval pattern: influential subordinate families could acquire independent ruling authority when an older dynasty declined.

The Vaghela period extended beyond the central early-medieval phase considered here. For the present topic, it is sufficient to recognise the succession and not confuse it with the earlier Chavda and Chaulukya stages.

Prelims focus

  • Vanraj Chavda is traditionally associated with the foundation of Anhilwad Patan around 756 CE.
  • Mularaja is associated with the establishment of Chaulukya or Solanki power in Gujarat.
  • The Modhera Sun Temple is associated with Bhima I and approximately 1026 CE.
  • Rani ki Vav is an 11th-century stepwell at Patan, traditionally associated with Queen Udayamati.
  • Hemachandra is associated with the Chaulukya cultural world, including Siddharaja Jayasimha and Kumarapala.
  • Trap: Bhima I belongs to the Gujarat Chaulukyas; he must not be confused with the different Chalukya rulers of Badami.

[Sources: GCERT, Social Science, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Rajput Age: New Ruler and States', section on Gujarat; GCERT, History, Class 11, ch. 13, 'Rajput States of India', section 'Gujarat', printed pp. 102–103; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, ch. 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture', printed pp. 75–76; Archaeological and cultural description in Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, 'Sun Temple at Modhera (Gujarat)' (online, consulted 19 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat', site description and inscription information (online, consulted 19 November 2026); Gujarat Tourism, 'Rani ki Vav', historical description (online, consulted 19 November 2026).]
